presentation: A fictional 58-year-old patient is brought to the emergency department with a 3-hour history of substernal chest pressure radiating to the left arm, accompanied by diaphoresis and nausea. The patient has no prior cardiac history.
findings: ECG: ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF

questions.question: Which coronary artery is most likely occluded?

answer.text: The right coronary artery. ST-segment elevation in the inferior leads (II, III, aVF) localizes the injury to the inferior wall of the left ventricle, which is supplied by the right coronary artery in the majority of patients with right-dominant circulation.

reasoning_chain.text: ST-segment elevation in contiguous leads localizes acute myocardial injury to the wall those leads view; leads II, III, and aVF view the inferior wall.
In most patients the posterior descending artery arises from the right coronary artery (right-dominant circulation), so an inferior-wall infarct most often reflects right coronary artery occlusion.

teaching_points.text: Leads II, III, and aVF view the inferior wall of the left ventricle; ST elevation there indicates inferior-wall injury.
Coronary dominance is determined by which artery gives rise to the posterior descending artery; roughly 70-80% of people are right-dominant.
